13903: Egypt's imperial age (Dynasties 18–20), from the expulsion of the Hyksos under Ahmose I to the end of the Ramesside kings. Pharaohs such as Thutmose III and Ramesses II controlled Canaan through vassal city-states, and the Amarna letters and Merneptah Stele come from this period. The exodus is set within it on both the early (c. 1446 BC) and late (c. 1260 BC) chronologies.
13905: An Anatolian power centred on Hattusa that rivalled Egypt for Syria, fighting Ramesses II at Kadesh (1274 BC) before signing the earliest known peace treaty. Its vassal-treaty form is often compared with the covenant structure of Deuteronomy. It collapsed in the Bronze Age crisis c. 1180 BC; "Hittites" in the patriarchal stories may refer to smaller groups in Canaan.
13907: From its heartland on the upper Tigris (Assur, Nimrud, Nineveh), Assyria built the first great Near Eastern empire using mass deportation. Shalmaneser III fought Ahab at Qarqar (853 BC), Tiglath-pileser III annexed Galilee, Samaria fell in 722 BC, and Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC. Nineveh fell in 612 BC and the last remnant at Haran in 609 BC.
13909: Founded by Nabopolassar, it overthrew Assyria and, under Nebuchadnezzar II, defeated Egypt at Carchemish (605 BC), deported Judah's leaders (597 BC) and destroyed Jerusalem (586 BC). Daniel and Ezekiel served among the exiles. Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC.
13911: Cyrus the Great united Medes and Persians and took Babylon in 539 BC, permitting the exiles to return. Darius I and Artaxerxes I appear in Ezra and Nehemiah; Xerxes is the Ahasuerus of Esther. Governed from Susa, Persepolis and Ecbatana through satrapies, it stretched from Egypt to the Indus until Alexander conquered it.
13913: Alexander the Great, king of Macedon, overran the Persian empire from 334 BC, taking Tyre, Gaza and Egypt in 332 BC and reaching India. His early death in 323 BC left the empire to his generals. Greek language and culture spread across the east, setting the stage for the Septuagint and the Greek New Testament.
13915: The dynasty of Ptolemy I ruled Egypt from Alexandria and held Judea until 198 BC. Alexandria became the greatest centre of Jewish life outside the land and the home of the Septuagint. It ended with Cleopatra VII and Roman annexation in 30 BC.
13917: Founded by Seleucus I and ruled from Antioch and Seleucia, it took Judea from the Ptolemies in 198 BC. Antiochus IV's attempt to suppress Judaism in 167 BC provoked the Maccabean revolt. Shrinking steadily, its last remnant was annexed by Pompey in 63 BC.
13919: The independent Jewish state founded by the Maccabean family, ruling as high priests and later kings. It expanded over Idumea, Samaria and Galilee, became a Roman client after Pompey's intervention in 63 BC, and ended when Herod the Great took Jerusalem in 37 BC.
13921: From Augustus to the deposition of the last western emperor in 476, Rome ruled the whole Mediterranean. Jesus was crucified under the prefect Pontius Pilate; Paul used Roman roads and citizenship; Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70. Persecuted at times, Christianity was legalized in 313 and became the state religion under Theodosius (380). The Republic had dominated Judea since 63 BC.
13923: The eastern Roman Empire governed from Constantinople, host of most ecumenical councils and heartland of Orthodox Christianity. It lost the Levant and Egypt to the Arabs in the 7th century, was sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204, and fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
13925: After Muhammad's death the caliphs conquered the Levant, Egypt, Persia, North Africa and Spain. Jerusalem fell in 637/638 and the Dome of the Rock was built in 691. Ancient churches of the east lived as protected minorities. The Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad ended with the Mongol sack of 1258.
13927: A Turkish dynasty that took Constantinople in 1453 and ruled Anatolia, the Balkans, the Levant, Egypt and Arabia, including Jerusalem from 1517 to 1917. Orthodox and other Christians were governed through the millet system. It was dissolved after the First World War.
